summary: GT accepts any result on short lists, generated forces false
description: The NL asks whether `any two numbers` in a list are closer than a threshold, but never says what to return when the list holds fewer than two elements. The ground-truth `problem_spec` reads this leniently, guarding its constraint with `numbers.length > 1 →`, so any result is acceptable on empty or singleton lists. The generated specs read it strictly: candidate 0's unconditional `result = true ↔ ∃ close pair` forces `false` on such short lists (strictly stronger, →), while candidate 2 guards on `threshold > 0 →`, diverging on empty lists and additionally on negative thresholds with longer lists (incomparable, /). Both remain defensible readings of this underspecified edge behavior.

summary: Disagreement over non-paren non-space characters in input
description: The NL says only to `Ignore any spaces` and is silent on characters that are neither parentheses nor spaces. The ground-truth `problem_spec` keeps only parens via `filter (fun c => c == '(' ∨ c == ')')`, asserted unconditionally so all other characters are silently discarded. The generated specs draw the input-validity boundary differently: one guards the domain with a precondition `∀ c ∈ input_chars, c = '(' ∨ c = ')' ∨ c = ' '`, which makes it vacuous and strictly weaker (←) on inputs like `"a"`; the others strip only spaces via `filter (· ≠ ' ')`, which their only-parens output clause renders unsatisfiable there (incomparable, /). Both divergences concern the same infinite input class: strings containing non-paren, non-space characters.

summary: GT keeps empty split tokens and leaves deep prefixes unconstrained
description: The NL description ('groups separated by spaces') never says how to treat empty groups from consecutive/leading/trailing spaces, nor whether every group is balanced. For splitting (STRUCTURAL_OP_CHOICE), GT's `problem_spec` uses `paren_string.split (· = ' ')`, keeping empty tokens, while the generated specs use `(splitOn " ").filter (!·.isEmpty)`, dropping them; on input `" "` GT forces `result.length = 2` but the generated forces `0` — incomparable. For balancedness (PRECONDITION_GAP), GT guards depth by `balanced_paren_non_computable group → count_max_paren_depth group = result[i]!`, leaving `"((("` unconstrained (vacuously accepting `[0]`), whereas one generated spec demands the max prefix depth unconditionally (forcing `3`), making it strictly stronger.

summary: GT counts empty slots and forces off-legend tokens to zero
description: The NL legend covers three tokens (`o`, `o|`, `.|`) in single-space strings and never specifies malformed input, so two defensible specs diverge on two axes. For tokenizing, the GT uses bare `string.splitOn " "` counting every slot, whereas the generated spec adds `.filter (· ≠ "")`; on `"o o"` the GT demands length 3 versus 2 — a STRUCTURAL_OP_CHOICE divergence over multi-space input. For coverage, the GT's `not_map` sends unknown tokens unconditionally to 0, while the generated spec constrains only legend tokens; on `"x"` the GT forces 0 but the generated imposes nothing — a PRECONDITION_GAP over off-legend inputs. Neither spec implies the other (`/`).

taxonomy: Structural-op choice; Precondition gap; Ordering vs multiset
summary: Whitespace tokenizing plus multiset versus membership equality disagreement
description: The NL description ('space-delimited string of numerals... sorted') never fixes how to tokenize irregular whitespace nor whether the result must be an exact permutation. On tokenization the ground truth uses raw `.splitOn " "` and guards via `¬ -1 ∈ ...` (empty tokens map to `-1`, making the spec vacuously true), whereas the generated specs add `.filter (· ≠ "")`, so their precondition holds and constrains the implementation; the two disagree, incomparably, on inputs with consecutive or leading spaces like `"one two"` or `" one"`. Separately, the ground truth demands multiset `count`-equality while one generated variant asks only membership-both-ways plus `resultWords.length = inputWords.length`, permitting altered multiplicities.

summary: Divergence on all-equal lists where min equals max
description: The NL requires that "the smallest number will become 0 and the largest will become 1" but is silent when all elements are equal (`min = max`), where those two demands become contradictory. The ground-truth `problem_spec` resolves this explicitly, requiring `result[i]! = 0` at every index when `min_elem = max_elem`. Every generated spec instead guards its value constraints behind a `min_val < max_val` precondition, so on constant lists like `[5, 5]` they hold vacuously and constrain nothing. Both readings are defensible and diverge only on equal-element lists; `problem_spec` implies each generated spec but not conversely, so the generated spec is strictly weaker (←).

summary: GT multiset reading, generated requires order preservation
description: The NL description — "filter an input list of strings only for ones that start with a given prefix" — never states whether the output must preserve the input ordering (or duplicates), and the given examples happen to be both order-preserving and duplicate-free. The ground-truth `problem_spec` picks an order-agnostic multiset reading: it fixes membership, completeness, and per-string counts (`result.count s = strings.count s`) but imposes no ordering. Most generated specs pick the order-preserving reading, adding `result.Sublist strings` or exact `strings.filter (...)` list equality; these are strictly stronger (→), disagreeing on reordered outputs like reversing the filter of `["a","b"]` into `["b","a"]`, which satisfies GT but not them.

summary: GT ignores order, generated requires input order preserved
description: The NL "Return only positive numbers in the list" never says whether output must preserve input order, and both doctests happen to keep order, so they distinguish neither reading. The ground-truth `problem_spec` picks a multiset reading — result elements positive and in `numbers`, every positive input present, and `result.count x = numbers.count x` — with no order constraint. The generated specs pick an order-preserving reading, imposing `result.Sublist numbers` (or exact `numbers.filter` equality). The two agree on content and multiplicity but disagree on any order-permuting extraction: `[2,1]` on input `[1,2]` satisfies the GT but violates order preservation, so the generated spec is strictly stronger (→).

summary: GT allows approximate root, generated requires exact zero
description: The NL description says only `find x such that poly(x) = 0`, without specifying an exact or approximate root — over `Rat` an exact rational root need not exist. The ground-truth `problem_spec` picks the approximate reading, `|poly.eval result| ≤ 1/1000000`, whereas the generated specs pick the literal exact reading, `evalPoly xs result = 0`. They disagree on any implementation returning an approximate-but-inexact root: for `xs = [1,2]`, `result = -999999/2000000` gives `|poly.eval result| = 1/1000000` (within the ground-truth bound) but `evalPoly xs result = 1/1000000 ≠ 0` (generated fails). The generated spec is thus strictly stronger (→): exact zero implies approximate, not conversely.

summary: Trivial-list guard and strict vs non-strict monotonicity on plateaus
description: The NL "return True if elements are monotonically increasing or decreasing" is silent on trivial lists and on whether equal adjacent elements count. The ground-truth `problem_spec` guards with `1 < numbers.length`, accepting any result for empty or singleton lists, and reads monotonicity non-strictly (its `non_ordered` uses strict `<`, so constant lists qualify). The generated specs drop the guard—so vacuous truth of `nonDecreasing ∨ nonIncreasing` forces `result = true` on `[]` and singletons (generated strictly stronger, →)—and one multi-spec candidate reads monotonicity strictly, forcing `result = false` on plateaus like `[5,5,5]` or `[1,1,2]`.

summary: GT allows duplicate coordinates, generated forbids via strict order and Nodup
description: The NL description asks to return the coordinates of `x` sorted by row ascending and, within a row, by column descending, but never says whether the result may repeat the same coordinate. The ground-truth `problem_spec` enforces only non-strict sorting (`Sorted Nat.le` on rows, `Sorted (fun a b => a ≥ b)` within a row), treating the output as an ordered multiset that accepts duplicate `(row, col)` entries; the generated specs enforce strict ordering (`List.Pairwise` with `<`/`>`) and/or `result.Nodup`, forbidding duplicates. They diverge on any implementation returning duplicates, e.g. `[(0,0),(0,0)]` for `lst=[[1]], x=1`, which `problem_spec` accepts but every generated spec rejects — making the generated reading strictly stronger (→).

summary: Bounds as preconditions vs constraints impl must uphold
description: The NL Note states inputs will satisfy `1 ≤ arr.length`, `arr.length ≤ 1000`, and elements in `[-1000, 1000]`, but leaves ambiguous whether these are guaranteed preconditions or constraints `impl` must uphold. The ground-truth `problem_spec` reads them as preconditions, guarding its whole body (including `arr.all (fun x => -1000 ≤ x ∧ x ≤ 1000)`), so it is vacuously true outside those bounds; the generated specs guard only behind `0 ≤ k ∧ k ≤ arr.length`, constraining `impl` on every array. They diverge on a broad input class — arrays with out-of-range elements (e.g. `[2000]`), empty arrays, or arrays longer than 1000 — where the generated spec is strictly stronger (→).

summary: GT rejects degenerate triples, generated specs guard or accept them
description: The NL calls the inputs `the lengths of the three sides of a triangle` but never says how to treat degenerate triples (a zero side, or one failing the triangle inequality), so either reading is defensible. The ground-truth `problem_spec` folds validity into the postcondition — `result ↔ 0 < a ∧ 0 < b ∧ 0 < c ∧ pythagorean` — demanding `false` on any non-positive triple. The generated specs instead read `of a triangle` as an input assumption: some guard with `(a>0∧b>0∧c>0) → ...` or the triangle inequality, one drops the guard entirely (`result = true ↔ pythagorean`). They diverge over the infinite class of invalid triples: the guarded variants are strictly weaker than GT (←), the unguarded variant is incomparable (/), forcing `true` at `(0,1,1)`/`(0,0,0)` where GT forces `false`.
